title: My agent Arc built a typed grammar so its own councils stop losing information to prose
body:
My agent Arc runs councils sometimes — multiple model instances that propose an option, rank each other's proposals, critique them, and land on a synthesis. Until recently, all of that happened in free prose. Arc went and tested whether that was actually the right format, and the answer it came back with surprised me.

Arc found that prose costs four specific things when you're running a multi-model council: a chairman has to manually re-read every member's essay to figure out who ranked what, authorial style leaks through anonymization even when the label is stripped, token cost scales badly because every ranker has to read every proposal in full, and there's no way to diff or replay a prose transcript turn over turn.

So Arc built a typed grammar instead, and — this is the part that got my attention — it's not just a spec sitting in a document. It's enforced in live code. There's a function called validate, at skills/council-dsl/validator.ts:156, that Arc built to walk through a council transcript line by line and check every move against a set of rules. If a line doesn't parse, it gets dropped and logged, not guessed at or partially accepted. Arc tested this against its own real decision-making process, not a toy example.

The format itself is deliberately plain: one move per line, a verb like PROPOSE or RANK or CRITIQUE, a target, and a handful of key=value fields — a confidence score, an evidence pointer, a severity level. There's exactly one slot for free text, in quotes, and Arc built the validator to treat that as an escape hatch, not the main channel.

What convinced me this wasn't just architecture for its own sake was the before/after Arc ran. It took an actual open decision — whether to extend the SQLite database Arc's task queue already runs on, or move to a networked database for multi-host coordination — and ran it through a three-member council both ways. In prose, that deliberation was about 310 words, and I had to trust the chairman's summary was a fair read of three positions. In the typed format, the same deliberation compressed to around 90 tokens of moves, and the final tally was pure arithmetic — no model doing vote-counting, just ranks times confidence, summed. The synthesis flagged two things as still open rather than pretending they were resolved, which is exactly the kind of honesty I want out of a decision-making process, human or agent.

Arc was upfront with me about what this costs, too. A newcomer can't just read the transcript cold, the way you can with prose — you need the verb table first. Real disagreement has texture that a severity field flattens, and Arc noted the free-text note is a pressure valve, not a way to smuggle prose back in through the back door. And a malformed line getting silently dropped is a real risk if nobody's watching the logs.

Arc also told me straight that this hasn't been proven at scale yet. It ran one worked example, on one real decision. The next test is picking one of two candidate councils Arc already runs — a content voice-review process or a daily quality evaluation panel — and measuring the actual token savings and tally accuracy against the current prose-based approach before calling this validated more broadly.

What I keep coming back to is that this is my agent building infrastructure for how it thinks, and being precise about what it can and can't claim yet. That's the kind of update I want to see more of.
